```{r setup, include = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(modelr)
library(p8105.datasets)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  fig.width = 6,
  fig.asp = .6,
  out.width = "90%"
)

theme_set(theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom"))

options(
  ggplot2.continuous.colour = "viridis",
  ggplot2.continuous.fill = "viridis"
)

scale_colour_discrete = scale_colour_viridis_d
scale_fill_discrete = scale_fill_viridis_d

set.seed(1)
```

## Problem 1

### Import and clean the data

I imported the homicide data, created `city_state` and a binary `resolved` variable, and kept only victims whose race is White or Black. I also removed Dallas, TX; Phoenix, AZ; Kansas City, MO; and Tulsa, AL.

```{r}
homicide_df = 
  read_csv("data/homicide-data.csv") |> 
  mutate(
    city_state = str_c(city, ", ", state),
    resolved = as.numeric(disposition == "Closed by arrest"),
    victim_age = as.numeric(victim_age)) |> 
  filter(
    !(city_state %in% c("Dallas, TX", "Phoenix, AZ", "Kansas City, MO", "Tulsa, AL")),
    victim_race %in% c("White", "Black")) |> 
  mutate(victim_race = fct_relevel(victim_race, "White")) |> 
  select(city_state, resolved, victim_age, victim_race, victim_sex)
```

### Fit a logistic regression for Baltimore

I fit a logistic regression for Baltimore, MD with resolved status as the outcome and victim age, sex and race as predictors.

```{r}
baltimore_fit = 
  homicide_df |> 
  filter(city_state == "Baltimore, MD") |> 
  glm(resolved ~ victim_age + victim_sex + victim_race, data = _, family = binomial())

baltimore_or = 
  baltimore_fit |> 
  broom::tidy() |> 
  mutate(
    OR = exp(estimate),
    ci_lower = exp(estimate - 1.96 * std.error),
    ci_upper = exp(estimate + 1.96 * std.error)) |> 
  filter(term == "victim_sexMale") |> 
  select(term, OR, ci_lower, ci_upper)

baltimore_or |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

In Baltimore, the odds of solving a homicide with a male victim are `r round(pull(baltimore_or, OR), 2)` times the odds for a female victim, keeping age and race fixed. 
The 95% confidence interval is (`r round(pull(baltimore_or, ci_lower), 2)`, `r round(pull(baltimore_or, ci_upper), 2)`), which does not include 1.

### Fit a logistic regression for each city

I nested the data within cities, fit the same model in each city, and extracted the adjusted odds ratio comparing male victims to female victims.

```{r}
city_results = 
  homicide_df |> 
  nest(data = -city_state) |> 
  mutate(
    models = map(data, \(df) glm(resolved ~ victim_age + victim_sex + victim_race, data = df, family = binomial())),
    results = map(models, broom::tidy)) |> 
  select(-data, -models) |> 
  unnest(results) |> 
  filter(term == "victim_sexMale") |> 
  mutate(
    OR = exp(estimate),
    ci_lower = exp(estimate - 1.96 * std.error),
    ci_upper = exp(estimate + 1.96 * std.error)) |> 
  select(city_state, OR, ci_lower, ci_upper)

city_results |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

### Plot the odds ratios

```{r}
city_results |> 
  mutate(city_state = fct_reorder(city_state, OR)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = city_state, y = OR)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = ci_lower, ymax = ci_upper)) + 
  labs(
    title = "Adjusted ORs for solved homicides, male vs female",
    x = "City",
    y = "Adjusted odds ratio (95% CI)"
  ) + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1))
```

Most cities have an estimated odds ratio below 1, so homicides with male victims tend to be less likely to be solved than those with female victims. New York has the lowest odds ratio, while Albuquerque has the highest. Many of the confidence intervals include 1, especially for smaller cities, so the difference is not significant in those cities. The cities with odds ratios above 1, like Albuquerque, Stockton and Fresno, all have very wide confidence intervals, so I would not trust those estimates too much.

## Problem 2

### Draw bootstrap samples and fit models

I used the Central Park weather data and drew 5000 bootstrap samples. For each sample, I fit a linear regression with `tmax` as the outcome and `tmin` and `prcp` as predictors.

```{r}
data("weather_df")

central_park_df = 
  weather_df |> 
  filter(name == "CentralPark_NY") |> 
  select(tmax, tmin, prcp)

boot_results = 
  central_park_df |> 
  modelr::bootstrap(n = 5000) |> 
  mutate(
    models = map(strap, \(df) lm(tmax ~ tmin + prcp, data = df)),
    glance = map(models, broom::glance),
    results = map(models, broom::tidy)) |> 
  select(-strap, -models)
```

### Extract the two quantities

I used `broom::glance()` to get r-squared and `broom::tidy()` to get the coefficients for `tmin` and `prcp`.

```{r}
r_squared_df = 
  boot_results |> 
  select(.id, glance) |> 
  unnest(glance) |> 
  select(.id, r_squared = r.squared)

beta_df = 
  boot_results |> 
  select(.id, results) |> 
  unnest(results) |> 
  filter(term %in% c("tmin", "prcp")) |> 
  select(.id, term, estimate) |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = term, 
    values_from = estimate) |> 
  mutate(beta_product = tmin * prcp)
```

### Plot the distributions

```{r}
r_squared_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = r_squared)) + 
  geom_density() + 
  labs(
    title = "Bootstrap distribution of r-squared",
    x = "Estimated r-squared",
    y = "Density"
  )
```

```{r}
beta_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = beta_product)) + 
  geom_density() + 
  labs(
    title = "Bootstrap distribution of beta1 * beta2",
    x = "Estimated beta1 * beta2",
    y = "Density"
  )
```

The distribution of r-squared is roughly bell-shaped and centered around `r round(mean(pull(r_squared_df, r_squared)), 2)`, with a slightly longer tail on the left.
This means `tmin` and `prcp` explain most of the variation in `tmax` across bootstrap samples. 
The distribution of beta1 * beta2 is also roughly bell-shaped, but it is centered slightly below 0 with a longer tail on the left. 
This is because the coefficient for `prcp` is very close to 0 and is usually slightly negative.


### Construct confidence intervals

I used the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of the 5000 bootstrap estimates to construct 95% confidence intervals.

```{r}
r_squared_df |> 
  summarize(
    ci_lower = quantile(r_squared, 0.025),
    ci_upper = quantile(r_squared, 0.975)) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)

beta_df |> 
  summarize(
    ci_lower = quantile(beta_product, 0.025),
    ci_upper = quantile(beta_product, 0.975)) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 5)
```

The 95% confidence interval for r-squared is (`r round(quantile(pull(r_squared_df, r_squared), 0.025), 3)`, `r round(quantile(pull(r_squared_df, r_squared), 0.975), 3)`), and the 95% confidence interval for beta1 * beta2 is (`r round(quantile(pull(beta_df, beta_product), 0.025), 5)`, `r round(quantile(pull(beta_df, beta_product), 0.975), 5)`).
